newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO considers future Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: NATO considers future Bosnia force.

text.p: NATO ambassadors began meeting on Monday to decide what kind of force to retain in Bosnia next year to bolster the shattered country's fragile peace.

After Washington declared on Friday it was willing to extend its presence in Bosnia for up to a year and a half, the ambassadors were expected to call for an international force of between 25,000 and 30,000 troops to remain in the region.
The mandate for the current NATO-led Implementation Force (IFOR) in Bosnia is to end on December 20, but most countries accept that a full withdrawal would hurl the country back into war.

NATO sources said the reduced force -- down from some 60,000 troops at IFOR's peak -- would have a "less intensive" presence in Bosnia, but would be strong enough to bolster efforts by civilian authorities to cement the Dayton peace accord.
"We will still have enough troops to deal with any trouble," one source said.

The ambassadors, who agree policy for the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, were to discuss four options for Bosnia, ranging from total withdrawal to keeping IFOR in its current size and form.
There is also the question of how long a new force would stay.
Washington has said it is willing to keep some 8,500 troops in the region, reviewing their situation every six months until the middle of 1998 at the latest.
Other countries have suggested the new slimmed-down IFOR remains on the ground for about a year, with its numbers being reduced throughout the period.

Although some countries, notably Germany, would like the force to have a wider mandate to hunt down alleged war criminals, NATO's military leaders are opposed to a policing role for the security force.
The ambassadors' recommendation, which is almost certain to be followed, will be put to NATO ministers in December.
